title: ZTE denial order activated
summary: BIS activated a suspended denial order against ZTE for seven years, to March 2025, after finding the company had lied about disciplining the employees responsible for illegal shipments to Iran and North Korea. The order barred all US persons from exporting anything to ZTE, which ended its supply of Qualcomm processors and its Android licensing and halted most of its production within weeks. ZTE settled on 8 June for a $1 billion penalty plus $400 million in escrow, a replaced board and a US-appointed compliance monitor.
gist: The first proof that one US order could shut down a large Chinese electronics firm.

title: ZTE denial order terminated
summary: BIS terminated the April 2018 denial order and removed ZTE from the Denied Persons List after the company met the terms of a superseding settlement: a $1 billion penalty, $400 million placed in escrow, a replaced board and a US-appointed compliance monitor. A ten-year denial order remains, suspended. The order had run for 89 days, and it is the only US measure on this timeline that barred exports outright.
gist: The only outright US export ban on this timeline lasted 89 days and ended in settlement.

title: Fujian Jinhua added to the Entity List
summary: BIS added Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit, a state-backed DRAM start-up, to the Entity List with a presumption of denial for all items subject to the EAR. The End-User Review Committee said the firm posed a significant risk of activities contrary to US national security, and BIS separately warned that new Chinese DRAM capacity threatened the viability of US suppliers of military memory. The listing stopped deliveries of Applied Materials, Lam and KLA tools mid-installation, and the fab never reached volume production. It was the first use of the Entity List against a Chinese memory maker and the model for later chip listings.
gist: US tool vendors walked away mid-installation and the DRAM fab never produced at volume.

title: Huawei and 68 affiliates added to the Entity List
summary: BIS listed Huawei Technologies and 68 non-US affiliates across 26 destinations, requiring a license with a presumption of denial for every item subject to the EAR. The listing ended Huawei's access to Google Mobile Services, Intel and Xilinx parts and US EDA tools. BIS added a further 46 affiliates in August 2019 and 38 more in August 2020, taking the listed total past 150 entities. Huawei's handset shipments fell from roughly 240 million units in 2019 to about 35 million in 2021.
gist: US suppliers now needed a license to sell Huawei anything, chips included.

title: Foreign Direct Product Rule extended to Huawei chip designs
summary: BIS amended General Prohibition Three so that foreign-made chips became subject to the EAR when they were the direct product of US-origin software or technology and were designed by Huawei or HiSilicon. The rule reached TSMC's production of HiSilicon Kirin and Ascend parts even though the chips themselves contained no US content. TSMC stopped taking new HiSilicon orders within days and stopped shipments after 14 September 2020. This was the first time Washington used control of US design tools to stop a foreign foundry serving a foreign customer.
gist: Washington used control of US design tools to stop TSMC building Huawei's chips.

title: Huawei FDPR broadened to any chip made with US equipment
summary: BIS widened the May rule so that any foreign-produced item made with US-origin semiconductor equipment or software needs a license when Huawei is a party to the transaction, whatever firm designed it. It also added 38 more Huawei affiliates in 21 countries and let the Temporary General License expire. Because almost every advanced fab uses Applied Materials, Lam or KLA tools, the rule made even standard merchant chips unavailable to Huawei. It established the equipment-based direct product test reused two years later for the China-wide rules.
gist: Because almost every advanced fab runs American tools, even off-the-shelf chips became unavailable to Huawei.

title: China's Export Control Law
summary: The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress adopted a single statute for export control, in force from 1 December 2020. It authorizes control lists, licenses, end-user and end-use certificates, a list of foreign parties that may be barred from buying, reach over reexports of Chinese-origin items and countermeasures against states that use export controls against China. Every Chinese export control since, from the gallium licensing of 2023 to the rare earth rules of 2025, is issued under it.
frCitation: Export Control Law of the People’s Republic of China, article 49
gist: The statute behind every Chinese export control since, passed two years before it was used.

title: SMIC added to the Entity List
summary: BIS added Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation and ten related entities to the Entity List, citing China's military-civil fusion doctrine and evidence of activities between SMIC and entities of concern in the Chinese military industrial complex. Licenses for items uniquely required for production at 10 nm and below carry a presumption of denial, while less advanced items are reviewed case by case. The listing ended SMIC's plan to buy an ASML EUV scanner, which the Dutch government had already declined to license since 2019. SMIC nonetheless reached a 7 nm-class node using multi-patterned DUV immersion by 2022.
gist: SMIC lost its shot at an EUV scanner but reached 7 nm with immersion DUV.

title: CHIPS and Science Act signed
summary: Public Law 117-167 authorized $52.7 billion for US semiconductors, including $39 billion in manufacturing incentives, $13.2 billion for R&D and workforce and $500 million for international supply-chain work, alongside a 25 percent advanced manufacturing investment tax credit. Companies taking incentives are barred for ten years from materially expanding advanced capacity in China or other countries of concern. Commerce's final awards included about $6.6 billion for TSMC Arizona, $4.745 billion for Samsung's Texas sites and $7.86 billion for Intel.
gist: Federal money for American fabs came with a ten-year bar on expanding capacity in China.

title: License requirement on design software for gate-all-around chips
summary: BIS carried out December 2021 Wassenaar Arrangement decisions on four emerging technologies. One of them, new ECCN 3D006, put a national-security license requirement on electronic computer-aided design software specially designed for developing integrated circuits with gate-all-around transistors, a structure the rule called key to processes at 3 nm and below. The rule was published on 15 August 2022, and the 3D006 control took effect on 14 October 2022. The requirement covers exports to China.
gist: Software for designing the newest transistor structure needed a license years before the 2025 letters.

title: First license requirement on A100 and H100 exports to China
summary: Nvidia disclosed in an 8-K that on 26 August 2022 the US government imposed a license requirement on exports to China, Hong Kong and Russia of the A100, the A100X and the forthcoming H100, plus DGX systems built on them and any future chip at equivalent performance. Nvidia put about $400 million of third-quarter China sales at risk. AMD received a parallel restriction on the MI250. Nvidia answered within weeks with the A800, which kept the compute but cut chip-to-chip interconnect from 600 to 400 GB/s.
gist: Nvidia lost its top China parts and answered within weeks with the cut-down A800.

title: October 2022 rules on advanced computing and semiconductor equipment
summary: BIS created ECCN 3A090 and imposed China-wide controls on chips above 4,800 total processing performance combined with interconnect bandwidth of 600 GB/s or more, capturing the A100 and H100. Equipment controls covered fabs making logic at 16/14 nm or below or with non-planar transistors, DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or below and NAND with 128 layers or more, with new foreign direct product rules extending them to non-US tools. US persons needed a BIS license to support advanced chipmaking in China. The interim final rule was published on 13 October: parts of §§742.6 and 744.23 and the new equipment ECCN 3B090 took effect on 7 October, §744.6 on 12 October, and the chip ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090, the direct product rules and the Entity List changes on 21 October.
gist: China lost access to top chips, the tools to make them, and American engineers.

title: NDAA section 5949 bars federal buying of Chinese chips
summary: Section 5949 of the FY2023 defense authorization bars executive agencies from buying electronic parts, products or services containing semiconductors designed or made by SMIC, ChangXin Memory or Yangtze Memory, or by their subsidiaries and successors, and from contracting with firms that use them. The bar takes effect five years after enactment, on 23 December 2027, and the FAR Council issued its implementing proposed rule on 17 February 2026.
gist: A procurement ban legislated in 2022 that does not bite until the end of 2027.

title: Micron barred from critical information infrastructure
summary: China's Cybersecurity Review Office, a body outside the export-control system, concluded that Micron's products carried serious security risks and ordered operators of critical information infrastructure to stop buying them, two months after opening the review. Micron told the SEC that customers headquartered in mainland China and Hong Kong were about a quarter of its worldwide revenue, and that roughly half of that revenue, a low-double-digit percentage of the worldwide figure, was at risk. It was Beijing's first direct retaliation against a US chipmaker. Chinese buyers shifted to Samsung, SK hynix and the domestic suppliers YMTC and CXMT.
gist: Beijing hit back at a US chipmaker for the first time and buyers switched suppliers.

title: Gallium and germanium export licensing
summary: MOFCOM and the General Administration of Customs issued Announcement No. 23 of 2023, placing eight gallium-related and six germanium-related items under dual-use export licensing from 1 August 2023 on national security grounds. Controlled items include gallium metal, gallium nitride, gallium arsenide, germanium metal, zone-refined germanium ingots and germanium tetrachloride. China produced roughly 98 percent of the world's primary gallium and about 60 percent of refined germanium at the time. Chinese exports of both metals fell sharply in the following months and ex-China prices roughly doubled.
gist: China showed it could squeeze the raw materials, and prices outside China roughly doubled.

title: Japanese controls on 23 categories of chipmaking equipment
summary: METI's amended export trade control order took effect, adding 23 categories of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment to the license list, covering cleaning, deposition, lithography, annealing, test and mask-related tools. The controls apply to all destinations, but a simplified process covers 42 friendly countries, so China is the practical target. Tokyo Electron, SCREEN, Advantest, Nikon and Canon were the main affected exporters.
frCitation: METI, amended export trade control order
gist: Japan's toolmakers now needed licenses to ship 23 types of advanced tools to China.

title: Dutch license requirement takes effect for advanced immersion DUV
summary: The Netherlands' national export control measure for advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment entered into force, applying to exports outside the EU on a case-by-case basis. ASML confirmed on 30 June 2023 that it would need Dutch licenses for all shipments of the TWINSCAN NXT:2000i and subsequent immersion systems, and said it expected no material impact on its 2023 outlook. ASML's 2024 annual report records higher shipments to China on a backlog built in earlier years, and customers in China represented 36.1 percent of its 2024 total net sales.
gist: The Hague could now refuse ASML's newest scanners, while shipments to China rose on an earlier backlog.

title: October 2023 update closes the A800 and H800 workaround
summary: BIS replaced the interconnect-bandwidth test with a performance-density criterion, splitting ECCN 3A090 into a controlled tier 3A090.a and a notification tier 3A090.b, which captured the A800, H800, L40S and even the RTX 4090. License requirements were extended to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5, which includes China, wherever they are located, and to further destinations in Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5, to stop transshipment. Equipment controls were tightened in a companion rule, which also made certain immersion lithography tools for advanced chipmaking subject to US export rules if they held any American content at all, unless the country they were first exported from already controlled them, and BIS separately added the Chinese GPU designers Biren and Moore Threads to the Entity List the same day. The rules were published on 25 October 2023 and took effect from 17 November.
gist: A density test caught the cut-down parts, and Chinese firms lost them wherever they bought.

title: Biren and Moore Threads added to the Entity List
summary: On the same day it closed the A800 and H800 gap, BIS added thirteen Chinese entities to the Entity List for developing advanced computing chips, among them Beijing Biren Technology and its affiliates and the three Moore Thread Intelligent Technology companies. A license is required for all items subject to the EAR, and applications are reviewed under a presumption of denial. Both firms had been designing GPUs meant to replace Nvidia parts in Chinese data centers.
gist: The two Chinese GPU designers closest to replacing Nvidia were listed the same day.

title: Dutch government partly revokes an ASML license for China
summary: ASML said on 1 January 2024 that the Dutch government had recently partially revoked a license for the shipment of NXT:2050i and NXT:2100i immersion lithography systems in 2023, affecting a small number of customers in China. ASML said it did not expect the revocation, or the latest US export rules, to have a material impact on its 2023 financial outlook.
gist: A license already granted for two of ASML's immersion scanners was partly withdrawn before the year ended.

title: Big Fund III capitalized at 344 billion yuan
summary: The third phase of the National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund was registered with 344 billion yuan, larger than Phases I and II combined. Six state banks together hold about 33 percent, with ICBC, Agricultural Bank, Bank of China and China Construction Bank putting in 21.5 billion yuan each. Reported priorities include silicon carbide and gallium nitride, high-value DRAM, and continued support for equipment and materials. Phase I raised 138.7 billion yuan in 2014 and Phase II 204 billion yuan in 2019.
gist: State money larger than the first two funds combined went toward tools, materials and memory.

title: Dutch controls extended to more DUV immersion tools
summary: The Netherlands expanded its national licensing measure to more types of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment with effect from 7 September 2024, taking over from the US license requirement that had covered ASML's TWINSCAN NXT:1970i and NXT:1980i immersion scanners and related services. Minister Klever cited increased security risks in the current geopolitical context and stressed that applications would still be assessed case by case. The measure was tightened again on 1 April 2025. The change consolidated control of the mid-range immersion fleet under Dutch national authority.
gist: Licensing power over ASML's mid-range fleet moved from Washington to the Dutch government.

title: Worldwide controls on gate-all-around, quantum and additive items
summary: BIS added worldwide license requirements for gate-all-around transistor technology under ECCN 3E905, for a set of quantum computing items, for scanning electron microscopes under 3B903 and for metal additive manufacturing equipment, aligning with controls that allied governments had adopted. License Exception IEC at §740.24 authorizes shipments to countries that have imposed equivalent controls, so the burden falls on everyone else.
gist: A worldwide control, with an exception for the allies who impose the same one.

title: December 2024 equipment and HBM package
summary: BIS controlled 24 additional types of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and three software tools, and for the first time controlled high bandwidth memory under ECCN 3A090.c, defined as memory with a bandwidth density above 2 GB/s per square millimeter of package or stack area, a line BIS said every HBM stack then in production exceeded. The rule excludes co-packaged chips that combine HBM and logic and whose main function is processing, which the chip controls may cover instead. New foreign direct product rules extended the equipment and HBM controls to production outside the United States, but the equipment direct product rule largely exempts tools exported by firms located in Japan, the Netherlands and the 31 other countries listed in Supplement No. 4 to Part 742. License Exception HBM at §740.25 still lets a US or Country Group A:5 exporter ship stacks below 3.3 GB/s per square millimeter directly to a packaging site for the designer that bought them. BIS simultaneously added 140 entities in China, Japan, South Korea and Singapore to the Entity List. The rules were published on 5 December 2024, effective 2 December, with compliance for the new ECCNs, the direct product rules and the DRAM definitions required from 31 December.
gist: High bandwidth memory came under control for the first time, wherever it is made.

title: Outright ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US
summary: MOFCOM Notice No. 46 of 2024, issued the day after the US equipment package, banned exports to the United States of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials and imposed stricter end-user and end-use checks on dual-use graphite. Unlike the 2023 measures, which set up licensing, this was a country-specific prohibition. The US Geological Survey estimated the gallium and germanium ban alone could cost the US economy about $3.4 billion of GDP. US germanium prices roughly doubled over the following year.
gist: Beijing switched from licensing to refusal, and American germanium prices roughly doubled.

title: AI Diffusion Rule announced
summary: The Framework for Artificial Intelligence Diffusion put a license requirement on the top band of accelerators, ECCNs 3A090.a and 4A090.a, to or within any destination worldwide, then reopened it unevenly. License Exception AIA carried them to the nineteen destinations listed in supplement no. 5 to part 740, eighteen allies and the United States. License Exception LPP carried 26.9 million TPP a year to a single consignee almost everywhere else, about 1,700 H100-class GPUs, and a license could take a country to a cumulative 790 million TPP through 2027, about 50,000. China, Russia and the rest of Country Group D:5 received neither exception. The rule also created Universal and National Validated End User authorizations for trusted data-center operators and, at ECCN 4E091, controlled the model weights of closed frontier AI models for the first time. Effective 13 January 2025 and published on 15 January with a compliance date of 15 May, it drew immediate objections from Nvidia and from allied governments.
gist: Top-band chips needed a license everywhere, and closed model weights came under control.

title: Dutch controls extended to measuring and inspection tools
summary: On 15 January 2025 the Dutch minister for foreign trade announced in the Government Gazette that from 1 April 2025 the national license requirement for advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment would cover further technologies, among them specific measuring and inspection equipment used in making advanced chips. The ministry described the addition as a very limited number of goods. It is the second amendment to the national measure since its introduction on 1 September 2023.
gist: The Dutch license requirement widened to measuring and inspection tools.

title: Foundry due-diligence rule and Approved IC Designer status
summary: BIS required foundries and packaging houses to apply a due-diligence test before making advanced logic dies, presuming that such a die is a controlled 3A090.a chip unless the designer is an approved or authorized IC designer or an approved OSAT attests to the package's transistor count. Until 13 April 2026, designers headquartered in Taiwan or Country Groups A:1 and A:5 counted as authorized without applying, a date BIS extended in April 2026 to 31 December 2026.
gist: The burden of checking who a chip is really for landed on foundries and packagers.

title: TSMC raises US investment to $165 billion
summary: TSMC announced at the White House an additional $100 billion of US investment on top of the $65 billion already committed in Arizona, for a total of $165 billion. The plan covers three more fabs, two advanced packaging facilities and an R&D center, taking the Arizona campus to six fabs. TSMC said the expansion would support around 40,000 construction jobs over four years. TSMC said its first Arizona fab had been in volume production since late 2024.
gist: Arizona is set to hold six TSMC fabs, two packaging plants and a research center.

title: Twelve more entities listed for AI and supercomputers
summary: BIS added twelve entities, eleven in China and one in Taiwan, for developing advanced AI, supercomputers and high-performance chips for Chinese end users tied to the military-industrial complex. A license is required for all items subject to the EAR, under a presumption of denial or a policy of denial. Companion rules published the same day brought the day's total to about eighty entities, covering exascale supercomputing, hypersonics and quantum.
gist: The listings moved from chip designers to the labs and supercomputer centers buying them.

title: Export controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths
summary: Announcement No. 18 of 2025 put samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium, together with their oxides, alloys, compounds and permanent magnets, under dual-use export licensing effective immediately, two days after the US reciprocal tariff round. China refines roughly 90 percent of global rare earth output and until recently accounted for about 99 percent of heavy rare earth separation. License processing initially ran to 45 working days or more, and Chinese magnet exports fell about 75 percent in May before recovering under a June trade truce.
gist: Chinese magnet exports fell about 75 percent in May before recovering under a June truce.

title: H20 and MI308 put under indefinite license requirement
summary: The US government told Nvidia that the H20, the China-compliant Hopper part designed to the October 2023 thresholds, would require a license for China, Hong Kong, Macau and D:5 countries indefinitely, on the concern it could be diverted to a supercomputer. The restriction also covers any chip matching the H20's memory or interconnect bandwidth. Nvidia warned of up to $5.5 billion of charges and ultimately booked $4.5 billion in the quarter, plus about $8 billion of lost orders in the next. AMD disclosed a charge of up to $800 million on its MI308.
gist: Washington pulled even the China-legal Hopper part, costing Nvidia billions in charges and orders.

title: BIS stops enforcing the AI Diffusion Rule
summary: Two days before the compliance date, Commerce announced it would not enforce the AI Diffusion Rule and would issue a replacement rule. Nothing was withdrawn from the regulations. License Exceptions AIA, ACM and LPP at 15 CFR 740.27, 740.28 and 740.29, the list of nineteen destinations in supplement no. 5 to part 740, the worldwide license requirement at 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) and the 790 million TPP per-country allocation at 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(B) are all still in the eCFR, and BIS confirmed in July 2026 that it enforces the worldwide requirement only against Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 and against entities headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. BIS issued three pieces of guidance the same day: that using Huawei Ascend 910B, 910C and 910D chips risks violating the EAR because they were likely made with controlled US technology, that allowing US AI chips to train or serve Chinese AI models carries consequences, and how exporters should guard against diversion. The Ascend guidance originally said the chips were restricted "anywhere in the world", wording BIS softened after Chinese protests.
gist: Enforcement stopped and deals took over, but every line of the rule stayed in the CFR.

title: Gulf AI infrastructure deals replace the diffusion caps
summary: During President Trump's Gulf trip the White House announced more than $200 billion of new US-UAE deals and an AI accord under which the UAE commits to build or finance US data centers at least as large and powerful as those it builds at home. The two governments separately announced a 5 gigawatt AI campus in Abu Dhabi led by G42, with reporting that the UAE could import the equivalent of roughly 500,000 Nvidia-class GPUs a year, about a fifth for G42 and the rest for US hyperscalers operating there. Saudi Arabia's new state AI company Humain signed agreements with Nvidia for several hundred thousand GPUs over five years and with AMD for a $10 billion program. The deals substituted bilateral, security-conditioned arrangements for the unenforced rule's country caps.
gist: Gulf states won large GPU flows by promising American data centers and security conditions.

title: Design-software sales to China put under license by letter
summary: On 23 May 2025 BIS informed Cadence that a license was needed to export, reexport or transfer electronic design automation software and technology where a transaction involved China or Chinese military end users. On 2 July 2025 BIS told Cadence that the requirement was rescinded with immediate effect.
gist: One letter cut China off from US design software, and another restored it about six weeks later.

title: H20 sales to China permitted again
summary: Nvidia said the US government had assured it that licenses for H20 sales to China would be granted and that it hoped to start deliveries soon; AMD received the same assurance for the MI308. Nvidia simultaneously announced an RTX PRO 6000D built for the Chinese market. Beijing then resisted: regulators raised security concerns with domestic buyers in August, told large firms to stop ordering the RTX PRO 6000D in September, and China's market regulator found in the same month that Nvidia had breached the conditions of its 2020 Mellanox clearance. Actual H20 shipments stayed small.
gist: Washington reopened the door and Beijing closed it, so few chips moved.

title: A 15 percent revenue expectation attached to China licenses
summary: The US government granted licenses in August 2025 that allowed Nvidia to ship H20 products to certain China-based customers. Nvidia's annual report records the condition that came with them: USG officials expressed an expectation that the government would receive 15 percent or more of the revenue generated from licensed sales of its products, but, in the company's words, "the USG did not publish a regulation codifying such requirement". No regulation codifying the payment has been published. Nvidia generated about $60 million of H20 revenue under those licenses. Its filing for the quarter ended 26 July 2026 says Beijing restricted the purchases and that Nvidia was unable to sell its H20 inventory. AMD was described at the time as accepting the same terms for its MI308, but has filed no comparable statement.
gist: Access to China now carried a payment demand with no rule or published legal basis.

title: US takes a 9.9 percent equity stake in Intel
summary: The US government bought 433.3 million Intel shares at $20.47 for $8.9 billion, about 9.9 percent of the company, funded by $5.7 billion of unpaid CHIPS Act grants and $3.2 billion from the Secure Enclave program. Counting the $2.2 billion already disbursed, the deal accounted for $11.1 billion of Intel's federal awards. The stake is passive, carries no board seat and the government agreed to vote with the board on most matters. It followed SoftBank's $2 billion investment and preceded Nvidia's $5 billion stake in September 2025.
gist: Unpaid grants turned into shares, making the government part-owner of an American chipmaker.

title: Validated End User status revoked for foreign fabs in China
summary: BIS revoked the Validated End User authorizations that let Samsung China Semiconductor, SK hynix Semiconductor (China) and Intel Semiconductor (Dalian), the NAND fab that SK hynix bought from Intel, receive US equipment for their China fabs under a single general authorization. The companies had 120 days after publication, to 31 December 2025, to obtain licenses. BIS said it would license the operation of existing fabs but would not approve capacity expansion or technology upgrades in China, and estimated the change would generate about 1,000 extra license applications a year. In December 2025 BIS granted SK hynix an annual license to ship approved US equipment to its China fabs during 2026.
gist: Korean-owned fabs inside China may keep running but may not upgrade or grow.

title: Huawei announces the Ascend 950 series with its own HBM
summary: At Huawei Connect in Shanghai, Eric Xu set out an Ascend roadmap of three new series over three years: the Ascend 950, 960 and 970. The 950 splits in two around memory. The Ascend 950PR, for the prefill stage of inference and for recommendation systems, uses HiBL 1.0, a Huawei-designed high bandwidth memory that the company presents as cheaper than HBM3E and HBM4E; Huawei said it would be available in the first quarter of 2026 as computing cards and in SuperPoD servers. The Ascend 950DT, for decode and training, uses HiZQ 2.0 with 144 GB of memory, 4 TB/s of memory bandwidth and 2 TB/s of interconnect bandwidth. Huawei said it built two kinds of memory because the inference stages have different needs.
gist: Huawei designed its own high bandwidth memory to feed its accelerators.

title: Affiliates rule extends the Entity List to subsidiaries
summary: BIS issued an interim final rule making any entity that is 50 percent or more owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more Entity List or Military End User parties subject to the same license requirements, worldwide. The rule closed the long-standing gap in which listed firms bought through unlisted subsidiaries. Industry warned it could bring in thousands of previously unlisted companies, and it brought Nexperia, owned by the listed Wingtech, into scope. Beijing called it a serious escalation and Washington suspended the rule for a year on 10 November 2025.
gist: Buying through an unlisted subsidiary stopped working, and the rule reached Nexperia.

title: Extraterritorial rare earth controls with a 0.1 percent rule
summary: MOFCOM Notice No. 61 of 2025 and its companions added holmium, erbium, thulium, europium and ytterbium to the controlled list, controlled rare earth mining, smelting, separation, magnet-making and recycling technology, and asserted jurisdiction over foreign-made goods in which Chinese-origin controlled rare earths account for 0.1 percent or more of value. Exports for foreign military users face denial and those for advanced semiconductor and AI uses face case-by-case review. It was the first time China applied a foreign direct product-style rule of its own. The 0.1 percent rule was due to take effect on 1 December 2025 and was suspended on 7 November, before that date arrived.
gist: China claimed reach over foreign goods, catching magnets and sputtering targets in chip gear.

title: Dutch government invokes emergency powers over Nexperia
summary: The Netherlands disclosed that on 30 September 2025 it had invoked the 1952 Goods Availability Act, a step it called highly exceptional, citing serious governance shortcomings at the Wingtech-owned chipmaker Nexperia. An Amsterdam court suspended the Chinese chief executive and placed the shares in trust. China retaliated by blocking exports from Nexperia's Dongguan plant, which packages roughly 70 percent of the company's output, causing shortages of automotive discrete parts across Europe. The Dutch order was suspended on 19 November 2025, and Wingtech later sought more than $8 billion in treaty arbitration.
gist: China answered by holding back Dongguan output, and European carmakers ran short of parts.

title: One-year truce suspends the affiliates rule and the rare earth regime
summary: Following the Trump-Xi meeting in Busan on 30 October 2025, BIS stayed the affiliates rule from 10 November 2025 until 9 November 2026. China acted first, in two steps: Announcement 2025 No. 70, on 7 November, suspended the October export control measures, including the rare earth rules, until 10 November 2026, and Announcement 2025 No. 72, on 9 November, suspended the December 2024 ban on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard material exports to the United States until 27 November 2026. China agreed to issue general licenses for US end users and their suppliers.
gist: Both sides stood their broadest measures down for a year, and China agreed to issue general licenses.

title: EU adds Dutch chip-tool controls to its own control list
summary: The European Union incorporated certain Dutch national controls into the EU Control List, extending to all member states a license requirement for specific semiconductor manufacturing equipment, through Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2003, which entered into force on 22 November 2025. ASML said in its 2025 annual report that this did not mean a change for it, because those products already required an export license from the Netherlands.
gist: Controls the Netherlands wrote alone became EU-wide, with no change for ASML's own shipments.

title: Trump clears H200 sales to China
summary: President Trump announced that the United States would allow the H200 and similar products to be shipped to approved customers in China. BIS announced the implementing rule on 13 January 2026 and it took effect on publication, 15 January, moving license applications for the Nvidia H200, the AMD MI325X and similar chips from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review, on conditions: the applicant must show that the exports will not reduce the global semiconductor capacity available to US customers, that the Chinese purchaser has adopted export compliance procedures, including customer screening, and that the item has passed independent third-party testing in the United States. Nvidia's filings state that the licenses require each H200 to pass a US inspection before shipment, so any H200 shipped under the program is subject to a 25 percent tariff on importation into the United States, which the company says it has been unable to pass on to customers.
gist: China could buy the chip, but only after US testing and a 25 percent tariff.

title: Section 232 proclamation puts a 25 percent tariff on advanced AI chips
summary: A presidential proclamation under Section 232 imposed a 25 percent tariff from 12:01 a.m. on 15 January 2026 on a narrow set of advanced computing semiconductors and products containing them that pass through the United States but are not destined for US use. The covered bands are chips of 14,000 to 17,500 total processing performance with 4,500 to 5,000 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, and 20,800 to 21,100 TPP with 5,800 to 6,200 GB/s, which capture the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X. Nvidia's H200 licenses require each China-bound chip to pass an inspection in the United States before shipment, so every licensed H200 is imported first and pays the tariff. Eight use-based exemptions cover US data centers, R&D, start-ups, repairs, consumer and industrial uses and the public sector. The proclamation ordered a review of data-center chips by 1 July 2026 and signaled a second phase with higher rates and an investment offset.
gist: A duty falls on chips crossing America for elsewhere, while American uses go free.

title: H200-class chips move to case-by-case licensing for China
summary: BIS announced the policy on 13 January 2026 and the rule took effect on publication, 15 January. It shifted license review from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review for exports from the United States to China and Macau of advanced computing chips with total processing performance below 21,000 and total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s, the band covering the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X. Approval is conditioned on certifications of adequate US supply, independent third-party testing inside US customs territory, and know-your-customer and remote-access safeguards. Because the testing condition routes the chips through the United States, they also incur the 25 percent Section 232 tariff. Blackwell-class parts remain outside the policy. The rule reached only the China and Macau branch of the license policy, at 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(A)(1); the worldwide license requirement and the presumption of approval for the supplement no. 5 destinations were left as they stood.
gist: A band below the top parts opened for China, with Blackwell still shut out.

title: US-Taiwan memorandum of understanding on investment
summary: The American Institute in Taiwan and the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office signed a memorandum of understanding on Taiwan-US investment, in which the United States committed to modify certain Section 232 tariffs on Taiwanese goods. Commerce and the US Trade Representative implemented the tariff elements on 28 May 2026, amending the tariff schedule for Taiwanese automobile parts, timber, lumber and wood derivative products and removing derivative Section 232 steel, aluminum and copper tariffs from Taiwanese aircraft components. A broader Agreement on Reciprocal Trade was signed by the two offices on 12 February 2026 but had not entered into force when the implementing notice was published. The notice records that under the MOU Taiwan will provide credit guarantees for up to $250 billion of corporate credit, and Taiwanese semiconductor and technology firms will make $250 billion of new direct investment in the United States.
gist: Taiwan won tariff relief on car parts, timber and aircraft components and pledged $250 billion of US investment.

title: Applied Materials pays about $252 million for shipments to SMIC
summary: BIS announced a settlement of about $252 million with Applied Materials and its Korean subsidiary over unlicensed reexports of ion implanters, classified under ECCN 3B991, to SMIC after SMIC's Entity List designation. The equipment was built in Massachusetts and routed through Korea, and the shipments were valued at about $126 million, so the penalty is twice the transaction value, the statutory maximum and the second largest in BIS history. Applied Materials agreed to multiple compliance audits and annual certifications, and the employees responsible no longer work for the company.
gist: A toolmaker paid twice what the shipments were worth, the second largest penalty BIS has levied.

title: Super Micro co-founder charged over AI servers diverted to China
summary: Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw, Taiwan-based general manager Ruei-Tsang Chang and broker Ting-Wei Sun with conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act, to smuggle goods and to defraud the United States. Prosecutors allege that a buyer purchased about $2.5 billion of servers from the manufacturer in 2024 and 2025 on false end-user records, and that at least $510 million of them were diverted to China between late April and mid-May 2025, using staged dummy servers to deceive auditors and layered transshipment. Liaw resigned from the Super Micro board the next day and pleaded not guilty on 1 April 2026; Super Micro shares fell about a third on the news.
gist: AI servers worth at least $510 million allegedly reached China through false papers and layered transshipment.

title: UAE moved to Country Group A:5
summary: BIS removed the United Arab Emirates from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and added it to A:5, granting Strategic Trade Authorization eligibility and license exceptions TMP, GOV, TSU, AVS and APR for chemical, biological and missile-technology controlled items. Licenses are still required for advanced computing items under ECCNs 3A090.a and 4A090.a, except when consigned to UAE government agencies, to approved commercial entities listed in a new Supplement No. 8, or to US-headquartered AI companies and their UAE subsidiaries including Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI. The rule put the bilateral model that replaced the AI Diffusion Rule's country caps into regulation.
gist: A named list of approved companies now governs Emirati chip access.

title: Proclamation 11052 sets a price floor and an extra duty on polysilicon imports
summary: A presidential proclamation signed on 6 August 2026 set a minimum import price of $100 per kilogram for polysilicon ingots and wafers and an extra 15 percent duty on imported ingots and other listed products made from polysilicon, both from 4 December 2026. Firms with Commerce-approved plans to build US polysilicon, ingot, wafer or cell plants, with construction starting by 20 January 2029, can import equipment and some of those products without the new duties. A Commerce rule published on 24 September 2026 to stop stockpiling before the duties start lists doped single-crystal silicon wafers among the products it covers.
gist: Imported silicon wafers face a price floor and an extra duty from December 2026, with relief for firms building US plants.

title: PRC restrictions leave the H200 licenses largely unused
summary: Nvidia's quarterly filing for the period to 26 July 2026 records that the US government began granting licenses in February 2026 to ship small amounts of H200 to specific China-based customers, but, in the company's words, "such sales were restricted by the PRC government, and we have been unable to sell all the products for which we have licenses". Nvidia took a $0.4 billion charge in the first half of fiscal 2027 for excess H200 inventory and purchase obligations, and shipped only a fraction of what the licenses allowed: less than 1 percent of data-center revenue in the quarter. Customers headquartered in China including Hong Kong accounted for $7.9 billion of the quarter's $96.2 billion of revenue, against $4.0 billion a year earlier. Beijing's own instruments are not published.
gist: Beijing restricted the sales, so Nvidia shipped a fraction and wrote down the stock.

title: China hits Japanese dichlorosilane with duties of up to 99.2 percent
summary: MOFCOM issued a preliminary anti-dumping ruling against Japanese dichlorosilane, a specialty gas used for thin-film deposition in chipmaking, requiring importers to post deposits with Chinese customs from 8 September 2026 at rates of 80.8 to 99.2 percent, with 99.2 percent for Shin-Etsu Chemical and all non-cooperating exporters. The investigation opened on 7 January 2026 after a complaint from Tangshan Sanfu Electronic Materials, and MOFCOM said the complaint's preliminary evidence showed import prices falling a cumulative 31 percent from 2022 to 2024. Japan protested the measure. The investigation is normally due to end by 7 January 2027 and can be extended by six months.
gist: Importers must now post deposits, making a Japanese thin-film gas costly for Chinese fabs.
